subject: english-language
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

learningObjectives.title: Reading non-fiction: retrieval, inference and synthesis
Analysing and comparing language, structure and perspectives
Vocabulary, sentence structure and technical accuracy in writing

questions.q: What is the title of OCR GCSE English Language Paper 1 (component J351/01)?
questions.explain: Component J351/01 of the OCR specification is titled 'Communicating information and ideas'.

questions.q: The reading section of OCR Paper 1 is based on which kind of source material?
options: A poem and a drama extract
One short story and one poem
questions.explain: Section A presents two non-fiction texts for reading, understanding and comparison.

questions.q: In non-fiction reading, 'explicit information' is best defined as information that is:
questions.explain: Explicit information is stated plainly on the page, unlike implicit meaning which must be inferred.

questions.q: A text says a volunteer 'skipped lunch again to finish the food parcels'. What can the reader infer?
options: The volunteer is dedicated and hard-working
questions.explain: Inference draws an implied meaning, such as dedication, from a detail rather than a directly stated fact.

questions.q: The exam asks students to 'synthesise' information from both texts. To synthesise means to:
options: combine ideas and information drawn from both texts
questions.explain: Synthesis (AO1) requires selecting and combining relevant evidence from across both texts.

questions.q: Which of the following statements is a fact?
options: This is the best report ever written
questions.explain: A fact can be checked and proved true, unlike the opinions in the other options.

questions.q: Which sentence is an example of opinion rather than fact?
options: Cycling to school is clearly the best way to travel
The new term begins in September
The bus fare is two pounds
questions.explain: 'Clearly the best' is a judgement that cannot be proved, so it is an opinion.

questions.q: Which of these is a non-fiction form?
questions.explain: An autobiography is a true account of the writer's own life, making it non-fiction.

questions.q: Comparing the two Paper 1 texts (AO3) mainly requires students to examine:
options: the writers' ideas and perspectives and how these are conveyed
the number of paragraphs in each text
the spelling accuracy of each writer
questions.explain: AO3 asks students to compare writers' ideas, perspectives and the methods used to convey them across texts.

questions.q: Listing three linked words or phrases together for persuasive effect is known as:
questions.explain: The rule of three groups three items to create emphasis and rhythm.

questions.q: A writer asks, 'How can we ignore a problem this serious?' The main effect of this rhetorical question is to:
options: prompt the reader to agree with the writer's viewpoint
request factual information from the reader
questions.explain: A rhetorical question invites the reader to share the writer's assumed answer rather than expecting a reply.

questions.q: Identify the technique used in: 'The city was a furnace that afternoon.'
questions.explain: The city is described as being a furnace directly, without 'like' or 'as', so it is a metaphor.

questions.q: When planning a piece of writing, the planning tool 'PAF' stands for:
questions.explain: Considering Purpose, Audience and Form helps a writer shape content, tone and structure appropriately.

questions.q: Which register is most appropriate for a formal letter to a local MP?
options: Standard English with a polite, formal tone
questions.explain: A formal audience such as an MP calls for Standard English and a respectful, measured tone.

questions.q: You must write to persuade your local council to build a youth centre. Which form and tone best suit the task?
options: A formal letter using persuasive techniques
A personal diary entry using slang
A private text to a friend
questions.explain: A formal letter matches the official audience and persuasive purpose of the task.

questions.q: A leaflet that uses commands, statistics and emotive language is most likely written to:
options: persuade the reader to take action
questions.explain: Commands and emotive language are persuasive devices aimed at influencing the reader to act.

questions.q: Which of these is a discourse marker used to signal contrast?
questions.explain: 'However' signals a contrast, while the others signal sequence, cause or addition.

questions.q: Why should a writer vary sentence lengths and structures in an extended response?
options: to create effect and hold the reader's interest
to use up the word count quickly
to avoid having to use paragraphs
to reduce the need for punctuation
questions.explain: AO6 rewards a range of sentence structures used for clarity, purpose and effect.

questions.q: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
options: My brother, who lives in Leeds, is visiting on Friday.
My brother who lives in Leeds is visiting, on Friday.
My brother who lives in Leeds; is visiting on Friday.
My brother, who lives in Leeds is visiting on Friday
questions.explain: The non-essential clause 'who lives in Leeds' is correctly enclosed by a pair of commas.

questions.q: For a formal report, which phrase is the most suitable replacement for 'a massive amount of'?
questions.explain: Formal writing favours Standard English vocabulary such as 'considerable' over informal phrases.

specSource: OCR GCSE (9–1) English Language (J351) specification; Paper 1: Communicating Information and Ideas
